CASE: Marmet Health Care Center, Inc. v. Brown, 565 U.S. 530 (2012) (per curiam)
FACTS: episodes/_planning/EP65_marmet_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md

ONE OPEN PROBLEM REMAINS (problem 1 closed 2026-08-04).

1. THE ENDING — CLOSED. Brown ex rel. Brown v. Genesis Healthcare Corp. ('Brown II'), 229 W. Va. 382, 729 S.E.2d 217, decided 2012-06-13 by Ketchum, C.J. Full text at measurements/EP65_brown_remand_RAW.md (CourtListener opinion 8182676, Harvard CAP capture; no syllabus in the capture). VERBATIM, checked against that file: 'In accordance with the Supreme Court's mandate, we overrule Syllabus Point 21 of Brown I. We otherwise find that the Supreme Court's decision does not counsel us to alter our original analysis of West Virginia's common law of contracts.' The state court gave up the one point it was reversed on and kept its unconscionability doctrine, which it describes as 'a general, state, common-law, contract-law principle that is not specific to arbitration'. THE DISPOSITION IS NOT UNIFORM — do not write 'all three were sent back': No. 35494 (Brown) Reversed and remanded; No. 35546 (Taylor) Reversed and remanded; No. 35636 (Marchio) Certified question ANSWERED 'Yes' (Section 15(e) preempted by the FAA), with unconscionability left to be raised on remand because the trial court never reached it. Nothing in Brown II says the clauses were finally held unenforceable; it returns that question to the circuit courts.

2. THE SECOND-PERSON FRAME IS UNSUPPORTED. 'The parent you admitted' assumes a relationship the record does not give. Only one patient is even named, and only in the caption. Either establish the relationships from another primary source, or rebuild the frame around what IS established: a family member signed, and the contract carved out exactly one kind of claim from arbitration — the nursing home's own claims to collect late payments. That carve-out is the strongest image the source supports and it needs no embellishment.
